store.0: I'm a fourth-year computer science major who loves coding and finds solace in my outside interests. I believe taking breaks and exploring hobbies helps me approach programming with a fresh perspective.
store.1: Sailing is a hobby that brings me a sense of freedom and challenge. It's a unique experience that allows me to disconnect from the stresses of college life and engage my problem-solving skills on a larger scale.
store.2: I'm a fourth-year Computer Science student who has seen the campus culture evolve over the years. I've discovered various communities that make this place feel like a second home. There are many ways to get involved beyond just coding.
store.3: I joined the Computer Science Society, which hosts weekly meetups to discuss new technologies, share personal projects, and have industry speakers. It's a welcoming environment for beginners. I can chat with fellow members who have worked on similar projects in internships.

store.0: I'm a Computer Science major, and I'm in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is really packed, but it's a good kind of busy. I'm finally taking the higher-level courses that I've been looking forward to for a while. It's surreal to think about how far I've come since my freshman year, when I was just learning about simple data structures. Now, I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even basic quantum computing. It's exciting to see how much I've grown and how much more I have to learn.

store.21: I've been involved in undergraduate research since the end of my sophomore year, and it's been a truly eye-opening experience. It's given me a glimpse into how knowledge is created in the tech world, and I'm proud to be a part of it. As a freshman, I didn't initially see myself going down the research route. I was more interested in coding projects and hackathons. However, one of my professors, who taught an introductory data science class, noticed my ability to bridge technical coding with user experience. She encouraged me to apply for a research assistant position in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific datasets. I was initially hesitant due to the intimidation factor, but I decided to take the leap. It turned out to be a great decision.

store.23: I'm a fourth-year Computer Science student who has seen the campus culture evolve over the years. I've discovered various communities that make this place feel like a second home. There are many ways to get involved beyond just coding.
store.24: I joined the Computer Science Society, which hosts weekly meetups to discuss new technologies, share personal projects, and have industry speakers. It's a welcoming environment for beginners. I can chat with fellow members who have worked on similar projects in internships.
store.25: I've been attending the VR/AR Club since my sophomore year. It's a great place to meet people who share my passion for immersive analytics. The club is very hands-on, with a VR lab in the engineering building where we can try out different projects. We also have demos where everyone shows off their latest projects, whether it's a mini-game or something more experimental. It's inspiring to see the creativity and excitement among the members. I feel motivated to push my own research further because of the supportive vibe in the club.
store.26: I occasionally attend events at the student-run radio station. They host open-mic nights where people sing, read poetry, or perform stand-up comedy. I remember one night, a friend from my Distributed Systems class performed an acoustic set. It was amazing to see him showcase his talent on stage. Moments like that remind me that there's more to someone than meets the eye when we're just coding together or working on group projects.
store.27: The central lawn is a popular spot on campus where students like to hang out between classes. Student organizations often set up booths there, promoting their clubs and handing out freebies like stickers or candy. I'm a sucker for free pizza, so if a club includes that in their advertisement, I'm easily tempted to sign up for their mailing list. The lawn is also where some of the biggest campus events take place, like our annual Tech Fest. During Tech Fest, different project teams showcase their prototypes and recruiters look for innovative ideas. It's a big deal here, especially for engineering and CS students.
store.28: I believe campus culture is generally collaborative. While there are competitive pockets, especially among seniors, people generally want to help each other succeed. The campus hackathon was a memorable experience for me. It brought together students from various backgrounds, from first-years to master's candidates, who spent 24 or 36 hours straight coding and learning from each other. It was chaotic but exhilarating. I formed a team with casual acquaintances, and the bond we formed during that all-nighter was incredible. We shared moments of triumph and frustration, and it created lasting friendships. That's the essence of campus life: shared experiences and challenges that bring people together.
store.29: Dorm life was a significant part of campus culture during my first two years. I lived in a dorm specifically for engineering majors, which we affectionately called "The Engi-House." The common lounge was always bustling with late-night coding sessions. You'd see someone working on an assignment for Data Structures while another group was streaming e-sports tournaments. It could get intense at times, with stressed-out engineers fueled by energy drinks. However, it also meant that if you encountered a problem, there was always someone nearby who could provide a helpful pointer. We'd also organize potlucks, watch Netflix together, or even host a talent show to unwind. It was a great way to build connections and create lasting memories.
store.30: I've been involved in volunteering at outreach events, particularly the "Tech for Good" day organized by our CS department. It's a great opportunity to share my knowledge and skills with local high school students who are interested in programming and problem-solving. By running mini-workshops on topics like web development or basic Python, I can help them gain a positive first experience in the tech world. It's incredibly rewarding to see them light up when they create a simple game or animated webpage. These events showcase a different side of campus life, highlighting the importance of community engagement and inspiring the next generation to pursue STEM fields.
store.31: I've found that specialized clubs are a great way to meet people who share your interests. My friend joined the Robotics Team in his first semester and found a second family there. They now hang out on weekends, watch movies together, and grab dinner. I've also formed close bonds with members of the VR/AR Club and the CS Society. We don't just talk about tech when we're together; we also joke around, complain about cafeteria food, and plan weekend trips to the local hiking trails. It's a great way to balance academics with socializing and create lasting friendships.
store.32: I'm excited and a bit anxious for Senior Week, which is a series of events leading up to graduation. It includes a formal dance, a carnival, and a day where seniors get their photos taken in caps and gowns around iconic campus landmarks. I've heard it's bittersweet because it's the last hurrah before everyone scatters. My older friends who graduated last year said it was one of the best weeks of their college life, filled with laughter, nostalgia, and a bit of sadness that the journey's almost over. I'm looking forward to making more memories and enjoying this special time with my fellow seniors.
store.33: The Rivalry Game is a big event on campus every year. Our sports teams face off against our biggest rival college in various sports, and it's a huge deal. Even if I'm not a die-hard sports fan, I love the energy on campus during that week. People show their school spirit by wearing colors, painting their faces, and carrying banners. The night before the big football game, we often have a massive pep rally with fireworks, which is a real spectacle. The vibe on campus is electric, and friends gather in dorm lounges or local bars to watch and cheer together. Whether we win or lose, it's a unifying moment for everyone, from business majors to art students to us nerdy engineers. We celebrate victories and commiserate losses together, creating lasting memories along the way.
store.34: The e-sports team has gained official recognition on campus, and it's been amazing to see the growth of the e-sports scene. The arena is equipped with a wide seating area and a big screen for streaming live competitions. It's not uncommon to see a hundred or more students gathering to cheer on our team during League of Legends or Overwatch matches. I never would have predicted that e-sports would become a legitimate campus institution when I started college, but it's a testament to the changing times and the evolving definition of competition and community. It's awesome to be a part of this vibrant and inclusive environment.
store.35: The "Midnight Breakfast" event during finals week is a great example of campus culture's ability to bring some fun and camaraderie to high-pressure times. It's a tradition where stressed-out students gather at midnight for pancakes and cereal, and it's a huge morale booster. Professors come to serve food, the school band might perform, and everyone takes a collective break from studying. It's a small thing, but it reminds us that we're not alone in feeling anxious about final exams. I appreciate how the campus culture makes an effort to ensure students have some enjoyment and a sense of community during tough times.
store.36: I believe campus life is what you make of it. If you're willing to explore, approach new people, and join clubs, you'll find a million ways to enrich your experience. It's easy to get lost in your workload, especially in a demanding major like Computer Science, but I've found that attending events, volunteering, and connecting with various communities has been incredibly rewarding. When I look back on my four years, I'll remember the late-night coding, but also the silly game nights in the dorm, the Tech Fest presentations, the hackathon adrenaline, and the excited cheers at the Rivalry Game. It's been a whirlwind, but I wouldn't trade it for anything. If you ever want a quick tour, I'd be happy to show you some of my favorite spots and introduce you to a few clubs. There's something for everyone here, and I'm glad I finally embraced all the campus has to offer.
